claim: SNc dopaminergic neurons were identified based on their location, size, and morphology.
source: SNc dopaminergic neurons were identified based on their location, size, and morphology (Figure 1A) and their characteristic electrophysiological properties, including a slow AP and the presence of a large sag in response to hyperpolarizing current pulses (Figure 1B).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the identification criteria used for SNc dopaminergic neurons.

claim: SNc dopaminergic neurons were identified based on their characteristic electrophysiological properties, including a slow AP and the presence of a large sag in response to hyperpolarizing current pulses.
source: SNc dopaminergic neurons were identified based on their location, size, and morphology (Figure 1A) and their characteristic electrophysiological properties, including a slow AP and the presence of a large sag in response to hyperpolarizing current pulses (Figure 1B).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the electrophysiological identification criteria.

claim: When post hoc tyrosine hydroxylase immunolabeling was performed, dopaminergic identity was confirmed in 100% of the cases (n = 121).
source: Independent of the developmental stage, these electrophysiological features allowed reliable identification of SNc dopaminergic neurons vs SNc GABAergic neurons: when post hoc tyrosine hydroxylase immunolabeling was performed, dopaminergic identity was confirmed in 100% of the cases (n = 121, see Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative data from immunolabeling experiments confirming neuronal identity.

claim: ISIavg was found to be stable from P2 to P29.
source: While ISIavg was found to be stable from P2 to P29 (Figure 2B,C), CVISI strongly decreased over the first two postnatal weeks, reaching a stable value by P10–11 (Figure 2B,D, Table 1, Figure 3).
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing no significant change in ISIavg across developmental stages.

claim: CVISI strongly decreased over the first two postnatal weeks, reaching a stable value by P10–11.
source: While ISIavg was found to be stable from P2 to P29 (Figure 2B,C), CVISI strongly decreased over the first two postnatal weeks, reaching a stable value by P10–11 (Figure 2B,D, Table 1, Figure 3).
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing a developmental decrease in CVISI.

claim: The decrease in CVISI was correlated with changes in firing pattern, with high CVISI values associated with a bursting pattern, intermediate values associated with irregular tonic firing and low values with regular tonic firing.
source: The decrease in CVISI was correlated with changes in firing pattern, with high CVISI values associated with a bursting pattern, intermediate values associated with irregular tonic firing and low values with regular tonic firing (Figure 2B).
evidence: The manuscript describes a correlation between CVISI values and firing patterns observed in the data.

claim: CVISI threshold values of 20% and 80% were found to reliably separate three types of firing patterns.
source: In fact, CVISI threshold values of 20% and 80% were found to reliably separate these three types of firing patterns (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific threshold values determined from the data analysis.

claim: All neurons were found to be bursters at P2–3.
source: Using these thresholds, the proportions of high CVISI (bursting cells), medium CVISI (irregular cells), and low CVISI (regular cells) were calculated for each developmental stage (Figure 2E): all neurons were found to be bursters at P2–3, most neurons were irregular between P5 and P11, while pacemaker neurons became predominant after P12 and were the only type of neurons encountered after P21 (Figure 2E).
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing the firing pattern distribution at P2-3.

claim: Most neurons were irregular between P5 and P11.
source: Using these thresholds, the proportions of high CVISI (bursting cells), medium CVISI (irregular cells), and low CVISI (regular cells) were calculated for each developmental stage (Figure 2E): all neurons were found to be bursters at P2–3, most neurons were irregular between P5 and P11, while pacemaker neurons became predominant after P12 and were the only type of neurons encountered after P21 (Figure 2E).
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing the firing pattern distribution between P5 and P11.

claim: Pacemaker neurons became predominant after P12 and were the only type of neurons encountered after P21.
source: Using these thresholds, the proportions of high CVISI (bursting cells), medium CVISI (irregular cells), and low CVISI (regular cells) were calculated for each developmental stage (Figure 2E): all neurons were found to be bursters at P2–3, most neurons were irregular between P5 and P11, while pacemaker neurons became predominant after P12 and were the only type of neurons encountered after P21 (Figure 2E).
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing the firing pattern distribution after P12 and P21.

claim: Rin and Cm displayed almost symmetrical changes over the first four postnatal weeks: Rin decreased while Cm increased.
source: Except for P2–3 where Rin values were particularly high (Figure 4C, Table 1), Rin and Cm displayed almost symmetrical changes over the first four postnatal weeks: Rin decreased while Cm increased (Figure 3, Figure 4C,D, Table 1), such that τm remained fairly constant over the same timeframe (Figure 3, Figure 4E, Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing opposite developmental trends in Rin and Cm.

claim: τm remained fairly constant over the first four postnatal weeks.
source: Except for P2–3 where Rin values were particularly high (Figure 4C, Table 1), Rin and Cm displayed almost symmetrical changes over the first four postnatal weeks: Rin decreased while Cm increased (Figure 3, Figure 4C,D, Table 1), such that τm remained fairly constant over the same timeframe (Figure 3, Figure 4E, Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing stable membrane time constant across development.

claim: After P2–3, membrane surface area increases but leak conductances' density stays fairly constant, such that the measured input conductance (1/Rin) scales with Cm.
source: These data suggest that, after P2–3, membrane surface area increases but that leak conductances' density stays fairly constant, such that the measured input conductance (1/Rin) scales with Cm (since Cm scales with membrane surface area).
evidence: The manuscript provides an interpretation of the passive property data based on biophysical principles.

claim: Both sag amplitude and rebound delay remained constant during the first four postnatal weeks.
source: In spite of the increase in amplitude of IH that has been described during postnatal development in SNc dopaminergic neurons (Washio et al., 1999), we found that both sag amplitude and rebound delay remained constant during the first four postnatal weeks (Figure 3, Figure 5B,C, Table 1), suggesting that the density of IA and IH remained fairly stable during this developmental timeframe.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing no significant change in sag amplitude and rebound delay.

claim: The density of IA and IH remained fairly stable during the first four postnatal weeks.
source: In spite of the increase in amplitude of IH that has been described during postnatal development in SNc dopaminergic neurons (Washio et al., 1999), we found that both sag amplitude and rebound delay remained constant during the first four postnatal weeks (Figure 3, Figure 5B,C, Table 1), suggesting that the density of IA and IH remained fairly stable during this developmental timeframe.
evidence: The manuscript infers stable channel density from the constant sag and rebound measurements.

claim: IH amplitude has been described to increase during postnatal development in SNc dopaminergic neurons.
source: In spite of the increase in amplitude of IH that has been described during postnatal development in SNc dopaminergic neurons (Washio et al., 1999), we found that both sag amplitude and rebound delay remained constant during the first four postnatal weeks (Figure 3, Figure 5B,C, Table 1), suggesting that the density of IA and IH remained fairly stable during this developmental timeframe.
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study reporting IH amplitude increase.

claim: AP threshold was found to not vary significantly during the first four postnatal weeks.
source: Except for AP threshold, which was found to not vary significantly during the first four postnatal weeks (Figure 6C, Table 1, Figure 3), most AP features were found to present significant modifications over the same developmental timeframe (Figure 3, Figure 6B–H, Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing no significant change in AP threshold.

claim: AP decay slope decreased over time.
source: Some of these properties presented monophasic changes, such as AP decay slope, which decreased over time (Figure 6B,F, Table 1), or AHP amplitude, which increased over time (Figure 6B,H, Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing a monophasic decrease in AP decay slope.

claim: AHP amplitude increased over time.
source: Some of these properties presented monophasic changes, such as AP decay slope, which decreased over time (Figure 6B,F, Table 1), or AHP amplitude, which increased over time (Figure 6B,H, Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing a monophasic increase in AHP amplitude.

claim: AP amplitude, rise slope and half-width displayed biphasic changes during the first four postnatal weeks, with the first change between P2–3 and P5 and a second opposite change between P8–9 and P13.
source: Surprisingly though, AP amplitude, rise slope and half-width displayed biphasic changes during the same developmental timeframe, with the first change between P2–3 and P5 and a second opposite change between P8–9 and P13 (Figure 6B,D,E,G, Table 1): AP amplitude and AP rise slope first decreased and then increased, while AP half-width presented an increase in value followed by a decrease.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing biphasic developmental trajectories for these AP properties.

claim: AP amplitude and AP rise slope first decreased and then increased.
source: Surprisingly though, AP amplitude, rise slope and half-width displayed biphasic changes during the same developmental timeframe, with the first change between P2–3 and P5 and a second opposite change between P8–9 and P13 (Figure 6B,D,E,G, Table 1): AP amplitude and AP rise slope first decreased and then increased, while AP half-width presented an increase in value followed by a decrease.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing the specific direction of biphasic changes.

claim: AP half-width presented an increase in value followed by a decrease.
source: Surprisingly though, AP amplitude, rise slope and half-width displayed biphasic changes during the same developmental timeframe, with the first change between P2–3 and P5 and a second opposite change between P8–9 and P13 (Figure 6B,D,E,G, Table 1): AP amplitude and AP rise slope first decreased and then increased, while AP half-width presented an increase in value followed by a decrease.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing the specific direction of biphasic changes.

claim: The different AP properties measured exhibit distinct evolutions, which suggest heterogeneous changes in expression or gating properties of the different types of ion channels involved in AP shape definition.
source: Therefore, the different AP properties measured exhibit distinct evolutions, which suggest heterogeneous changes in expression or gating properties of the different types of ion channels involved in AP shape definition.
evidence: The manuscript infers heterogeneous ion channel changes from the distinct developmental trajectories of AP properties.

claim: GS was found to gradually decrease over the first three postnatal weeks.
source: While GS was found to gradually decrease over the first three postnatal weeks (Figure 3, Figure 7C, Table 1), GE decreased mainly between P2–3 and P5 and remained stable afterwards (Figure 3, Figure 7D, Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing a gradual decrease in gain at start.

claim: GE decreased mainly between P2–3 and P5 and remained stable afterwards.
source: While GS was found to gradually decrease over the first three postnatal weeks (Figure 3, Figure 7C, Table 1), GE decreased mainly between P2–3 and P5 and remained stable afterwards (Figure 3, Figure 7D, Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing a specific developmental trajectory for gain at end.

claim: SFA index was found to be stable between P2–3 and P8–9 and then to drop to a steady value.
source: As a consequence of these different developmental timecourses, SFA index was found to be stable between P2–3 and P8–9 and then to drop to a steady value (Figure 3, Figure 7E, Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing the developmental trajectory of the SFA index.

claim: A first transition occurs between P2–3 and P5 while a second transition occurs between P8–9 and P12–13.
source: Although this table only represents independent uni-variate analyses of the changes in each firing property, the stacking of the statistical differences provides a first visual impression of where important transitions in electrophysiological behavior occur: a first transition occurs between P2–3 and P5 while a second transition occurs between P8–9 and P12–13 (Figure 3).
evidence: The manuscript identifies two developmental transitions from the statistical stacking analysis.

claim: The second transition was less clearly defined, spanning several of the developmental stages analyzed.
source: Therefore, the second transition was less clearly defined, spanning several of the developmental stages analyzed (a small number of statistical differences are still present between P10–P11 or P12–P13 and later stages).
evidence: The manuscript describes the characteristics of the second transition based on the statistical analysis.

claim: Outside of these transition phases, most electrophysiological parameters remain constant (between P5 and P8–9, then between P14 and P28).
source: Outside of these transition phases, most electrophysiological parameters remain constant (between P5 and P8–9, then between P14 and P28).
evidence: The manuscript identifies periods of stability in electrophysiological parameters.

claim: Using AHC with an automatic setting of the dissimilarity threshold, the 263 recorded neurons were separated into three classes of heterogeneous sizes.
source: Using AHC with an automatic setting of the dissimilarity threshold (XLSTAT software), the 263 recorded neurons were separated into three classes of heterogeneous sizes (Figure 8A).
evidence: The manuscript describes the results of the AHC analysis.

claim: Bursting, irregular and regular tonic neurons were clustered in separate classes (class 1, 2 and 3, respectively).
source: The observation of the recordings corresponding to the central objects of each class reveals that bursting, irregular and regular tonic neurons were clustered in separate classes (class 1, 2 and 3, respectively; Figure 8B).
evidence: The manuscript describes the firing patterns associated with each AHC class.

claim: CVISI was one of the parameters presenting the most significant differences between the central objects or the centroids of each class.
source: Unsurprisingly, CVISI was one of the parameters presenting the most significant differences between the central objects (Figure 8B) or the centroids (Figure 8C) of each class.
evidence: The manuscript identifies CVISI as a key discriminating parameter in the AHC analysis.

claim: AP half-width, AP rise slope, AP decay slope, and AHP amplitude also presented notable differences between the three classes.
source: Nonetheless, other parameters such as AP half-width, AP rise slope, AP decay slope, and AHP amplitude also presented notable differences between the three classes (Figure 8B,C).
evidence: The manuscript identifies additional parameters that differ between AHC classes.

claim: The mean ages were P3.5, P7.44, and P17.32 for class 1, 2, and 3, respectively.
source: Consistent with the developmental timecourse of firing pattern depicted in Figure 2E, the mean ages were P3.5, P7.44, and P17.32 for class 1, 2, and 3, respectively (Figure 8C).
evidence: The manuscript provides the calculated mean ages for each AHC class.

claim: AHC analysis based solely on spontaneous activity-related electrophysiological parameters clearly discriminates between the three developmental stages observed between P2 and P28.
source: Therefore, AHC analysis based solely on spontaneous activity-related electrophysiological parameters clearly discriminates between the three developmental stages (or electrophysiological behaviors) observed between P2 and P28.
evidence: The manuscript concludes that AHC successfully identifies developmental stages.

claim: The first two principal components (PC1 and PC2) accounted for ∼94% of the variance of the variables.
source: The first two principal components (PC1 and PC2) accounted for ∼94% of the variance of the variables (Figure 9A), and therefore were chosen for the two-dimensional representation of the developmental evolution of the 8 electrophysiological parameters during postnatal development.
evidence: The manuscript provides the variance explained by the principal components.

claim: CVISI and AHP mainly contribute to PC1.
source: The contribution of each electrophysiological parameter to PC1 and PC2 is represented in Figure 9A: while CVISI and AHP mainly contribute to PC1, other parameters such as AP amplitude, AP rise slope, AP decay slope, and AP half-width contribute to a similar extent to PC1 and PC2.
evidence: The manuscript describes the parameter contributions to PC1.

claim: AP amplitude, AP rise slope, AP decay slope, and AP half-width contribute to a similar extent to PC1 and PC2.
source: The contribution of each electrophysiological parameter to PC1 and PC2 is represented in Figure 9A: while CVISI and AHP mainly contribute to PC1, other parameters such as AP amplitude, AP rise slope, AP decay slope, and AP half-width contribute to a similar extent to PC1 and PC2.
evidence: The manuscript describes the parameter contributions to both PCs.

claim: ISIavg and AP threshold show minor contributions to both PCs.
source: Finally, ISIavg and AP threshold show minor contributions to both PCs.
evidence: The manuscript describes the parameter contributions to the PCs.

claim: The three classes identified by AHC were found to cluster in distinct regions of the PC1/PC2 space.
source: Consistent with the AHC results, the three classes were found to cluster in distinct regions of the PC1/PC2 space (Figure 9B).
evidence: The manuscript shows that AHC and PCA give consistent results.

claim: The developmental trajectory of the electrophysiological properties of SNc dopaminergic neurons is composed of two distinct phases.
source: Although age was not included as one of the parameters of the PCA, the mean PC1 and PC2 values and the associated standard deviations were calculated for each developmental stage analyzed, and could be represented in the PC1/PC2 space (Figure 9C): the distribution of values demonstrated that the developmental trajectory of the electrophysiological properties of SNc dopaminergic neurons is composed of two distinct phases, a first phase where PC1 and PC2 simultaneously decrease (between P2–3 and P5–11) and a second phase where PC1 keeps on decreasing while PC2 increases (between P11 and P15) (Figure 9C1).
evidence: The manuscript describes the biphasic developmental trajectory revealed by PCA.

claim: In the first phase, PC1 and PC2 simultaneously decrease (between P2–3 and P5–11).
source: Although age was not included as one of the parameters of the PCA, the mean PC1 and PC2 values and the associated standard deviations were calculated for each developmental stage analyzed, and could be represented in the PC1/PC2 space (Figure 9C): the distribution of values demonstrated that the developmental trajectory of the electrophysiological properties of SNc dopaminergic neurons is composed of two distinct phases, a first phase where PC1 and PC2 simultaneously decrease (between P2–3 and P5–11) and a second phase where PC1 keeps on decreasing while PC2 increases (between P11 and P15) (Figure 9C1).
evidence: The manuscript describes the first phase of the developmental trajectory.

claim: In the second phase, PC1 keeps on decreasing while PC2 increases (between P11 and P15).
source: Although age was not included as one of the parameters of the PCA, the mean PC1 and PC2 values and the associated standard deviations were calculated for each developmental stage analyzed, and could be represented in the PC1/PC2 space (Figure 9C): the distribution of values demonstrated that the developmental trajectory of the electrophysiological properties of SNc dopaminergic neurons is composed of two distinct phases, a first phase where PC1 and PC2 simultaneously decrease (between P2–3 and P5–11) and a second phase where PC1 keeps on decreasing while PC2 increases (between P11 and P15) (Figure 9C1).
evidence: The manuscript describes the second phase of the developmental trajectory.

claim: The electrophysiological behavior of SNc dopaminergic neurons in vitro reaches a steady state by P14–15.
source: Interestingly, PCA also reveals that the electrophysiological behavior of SNc dopaminergic neurons in vitro reaches a steady state by P14–15, and that no significant change is observed after this stage, although some variability in the electrophysiological properties might still be present (Figure 9C2).
evidence: The manuscript identifies the developmental stage at which maturity is reached.

claim: No significant change is observed after P14-15, although some variability in the electrophysiological properties might still be present.
source: Interestingly, PCA also reveals that the electrophysiological behavior of SNc dopaminergic neurons in vitro reaches a steady state by P14–15, and that no significant change is observed after this stage, although some variability in the electrophysiological properties might still be present (Figure 9C2).
evidence: The manuscript describes the stability of electrophysiological properties after P14-15.

claim: The electrophysiological development of SNc dopaminergic neurons is composed of two phases that involve changes in different sets of electrophysiological properties, most likely indicating that different ion currents evolve with distinct developmental timecourses.
source: Therefore, PCA demonstrates that the electrophysiological development of SNc dopaminergic neurons is composed of two phases that involve changes in different sets of electrophysiological properties, most likely indicating that different ion currents evolve with distinct developmental timecourses.
evidence: The manuscript infers heterogeneous ion current development from the PCA results.

claim: Phenotype is more variable at early than late developmental stages.
source: This analysis showed that phenotype is more variable at early than late developmental stages.
evidence: The manuscript describes the variability analysis results.

claim: The standard deviation of PC1 was found to be significantly and negatively correlated with age (r = 0.802, p < 0.001, n = 15).
source: Consistent with this analysis, and since PC1 accounts for ∼65% of the variance of our observations (vs ∼28% for PC2), the standard deviation of PC1 was found to be significantly and negatively correlated with age (r = 0.802, p < 0.001, n = 15).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical evidence for the correlation between variability and age.

claim: The multi-variate analyses reveal that the electrical phenotype of SNc dopaminergic neurons follows a progressively narrowing biphasic developmental trajectory.
source: In summary, the multi-variate analyses reveal that the electrical phenotype of SNc dopaminergic neurons follows a progressively narrowing biphasic developmental trajectory.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the key finding from the multi-variate analyses.

claim: Apamin application induced a decrease in AHP associated with an increase in CVISI, corresponding to a switch from regular to irregular firing.
source: As expected, apamin application induced a decrease in AHP (Figure 11A, Figure 11—figure supplement 1) associated with an increase in CVISI, corresponding to a switch from regular to irregular firing (Figure 11A).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing the effect of apamin.

claim: Artificially increasing Rin by the injection of a leak negative conductance amplified the apamin effect, resulting in the appearance of burst firing.
source: Artificially increasing Rin by the injection of a leak negative conductance amplified the apamin effect, resulting in the appearance of burst firing (Figure 11A), consistent with the results obtained by Paladini et al. (1999).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing the combined effect of apamin and leak subtraction.

claim: Apamin application and leak subtraction induced an electrophysiological regression of P8 neurons to a P2–P3 phenotype.
source: This analysis demonstrated that apamin application and leak subtraction induced an electrophysiological regression of P8 neurons to a P2–P3 phenotype (Figure 11B,E), each isolated manipulation accounting for roughly 50% of the change in electrophysiological phenotype.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing phenotypic regression.

claim: Each isolated manipulation (apamin or leak subtraction) accounted for roughly 50% of the change in electrophysiological phenotype.
source: This analysis demonstrated that apamin application and leak subtraction induced an electrophysiological regression of P8 neurons to a P2–P3 phenotype (Figure 11B,E), each isolated manipulation accounting for roughly 50% of the change in electrophysiological phenotype.
evidence: The manuscript quantifies the contribution of each manipulation to phenotypic change.

claim: The apamin/TTX application induced an increase in CVISI and a decrease in AP amplitude (and rise and decay slopes).
source: As shown in Figure 11C (see also Figure 11—figure supplement 1), the apamin/TTX application induced an increase in CVISI and a decrease in AP amplitude (and rise and decay slopes).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing the effect of apamin and TTX.

claim: The apamin/TTX application induced a phenotype switch quantitatively similar (and opposite in sign) to the one observed between P7 and P15.
source: This analysis demonstrated that the apamin/TTX application induced a phenotype switch quantitatively similar (and opposite in sign) to the one observed between P7 and P15 (Figure 11D,E).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing phenotypic regression from P14-16 to P7.

claim: SNc dopaminergic neurons switch from bursting to irregular to regular spontaneous activity pattern during the first three postnatal weeks.
source: In the present study, we characterized the development of electrophysiological behavior of rat SNc dopaminergic neurons in vitro over the first four postnatal weeks. We first demonstrate that SNc dopaminergic neurons switch from bursting to irregular to regular spontaneous activity pattern during the first three postnatal weeks.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes a key finding about developmental changes in firing patterns.

claim: The postnatal electrophysiological development of SNc dopaminergic neurons involves two major transitions occurring between P3 and P5 and between P9 and P11, respectively.
source: Using univariate analysis of 16 electrophysiological parameters (AP measurements, passive properties, excitability, etc…) and multivariate analyses (AHC and PCA) of 8 electrophysiological parameters, we demonstrate that the postnatal electrophysiological development of SNc dopaminergic neurons involves two major transitions occurring between P3 and P5 and between P9 and P11, respectively, and that mature in vitro electrophysiological behavior (regular pacemaking activity) is essentially attained by P15.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes a key finding about developmental transitions.

claim: Mature in vitro electrophysiological behavior (regular pacemaking activity) is essentially attained by P15.
source: Using univariate analysis of 16 electrophysiological parameters (AP measurements, passive properties, excitability, etc…) and multivariate analyses (AHC and PCA) of 8 electrophysiological parameters, we demonstrate that the postnatal electrophysiological development of SNc dopaminergic neurons involves two major transitions occurring between P3 and P5 and between P9 and P11, respectively, and that mature in vitro electrophysiological behavior (regular pacemaking activity) is essentially attained by P15.
evidence: The manuscript identifies the developmental stage at which maturity is reached.

claim: The two developmental transitions can be precisely reproduced by distinct manipulations of passive and active properties.
source: Using pharmacology and dynamic-clamp, we then demonstrate that the two developmental transitions can be precisely reproduced by distinct manipulations of passive and active properties, suggesting heterogeneous timecourses of development of the underlying ion channels.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes experimental findings about the biophysical mechanisms of developmental transitions.

claim: The two developmental transitions suggest heterogeneous timecourses of development of the underlying ion channels.
source: Using pharmacology and dynamic-clamp, we then demonstrate that the two developmental transitions can be precisely reproduced by distinct manipulations of passive and active properties, suggesting heterogeneous timecourses of development of the underlying ion channels.
evidence: The manuscript infers heterogeneous ion channel development from the experimental results.

claim: Mature SNc dopaminergic neurons can display regular tonic, irregular or bursting activity depending on the behavioral context in vivo.
source: In vivo, mature SNc dopaminergic neurons can display regular tonic, irregular or bursting activity depending on the behavioral context (Grace and Bunney, 1984a, 1984b; Tepper et al., 1990; Kitai et al., 1999; Grace et al., 2007).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies describing in vivo activity patterns.

claim: Variations in activity patterns are associated with a modulation of dopamine release such that immediate early gene activation is triggered only by bursting patterns of activity.
source: These variations in activity patterns are associated with a modulation of dopamine release such that, for instance, immediate early gene activation is triggered only by bursting patterns of activity (Kitai et al., 1999).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study linking activity patterns to dopamine release and gene activation.

claim: Regular tonic activity seems to rely mainly on SNc dopaminergic neuron intrinsic conductances.
source: From a biophysical point of view, regular tonic activity seems to rely mainly on SNc dopaminergic neuron intrinsic conductances while both irregular and bursting patterns necessitate the release of various neurotransmitters (glutamate, acetylcholine) by SNc synaptic inputs (Kitai et al., 1999; Grace et al., 2007).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies describing the biophysical basis of activity patterns.

claim: Both irregular and bursting patterns necessitate the release of various neurotransmitters (glutamate, acetylcholine) by SNc synaptic inputs.
source: From a biophysical point of view, regular tonic activity seems to rely mainly on SNc dopaminergic neuron intrinsic conductances while both irregular and bursting patterns necessitate the release of various neurotransmitters (glutamate, acetylcholine) by SNc synaptic inputs (Kitai et al., 1999; Grace et al., 2007).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies describing the biophysical basis of activity patterns.

claim: Mature SNc dopaminergic neurons mainly display a regular tonic (also called pacemaker) firing behavior in vitro.
source: In vitro however, mature SNc dopaminergic neurons mainly display a regular tonic (also called pacemaker) firing behavior (Grace and Onn, 1989; Liss et al., 2001; Seutin et al., 2001; Puopolo et al., 2007; Guzman et al., 2009; Putzier et al., 2009b; Tateno and Robinson, 2011; Amendola et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple previous studies describing in vitro firing behavior.

claim: The irregular pattern of spontaneous activity is observed in immature SNc DA neurons in vitro (postnatal days 9–16, P9–P16) and seems to be due to transient spontaneous activation of T-type calcium channels.
source: The irregular pattern of spontaneous activity is observed in immature SNc DA neurons in vitro (postnatal days 9–16, P9–P16) and seems to be due to transient spontaneous activation of T-type calcium channels (Seutin et al., 2000; Cui et al., 2004) and subsequent activation of calcium-activated potassium channels (SK) (Seutin et al., 1998; Wolfart and Roeper, 2002; Cui et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies describing irregular firing in immature neurons.

claim: The irregular pattern of spontaneous activity seems to be due to subsequent activation of calcium-activated potassium channels (SK).
source: The irregular pattern of spontaneous activity is observed in immature SNc DA neurons in vitro (postnatal days 9–16, P9–P16) and seems to be due to transient spontaneous activation of T-type calcium channels (Seutin et al., 2000; Cui et al., 2004) and subsequent activation of calcium-activated potassium channels (SK) (Seutin et al., 1998; Wolfart and Roeper, 2002; Cui et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies describing the mechanism of irregular firing.

claim: The spontaneous bursting pattern of activity is usually absent from mature SNc DA neurons in vitro, but can be observed in juvenile neurons (P15–P21) and depends on the activation of NMDA receptors.
source: Finally, the spontaneous bursting pattern of activity is usually absent from mature SNc DA neurons in vitro, but can be observed in juvenile neurons (P15–P21) and depends on the activation of NMDA receptors (Mereu et al., 1997), or can be promoted by pharmacological blockade of T-type calcium channels and SK potassium channels (Wolfart and Roeper, 2002).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies describing bursting activity in juvenile neurons.

claim: Bursting can be promoted by pharmacological blockade of T-type calcium channels and SK potassium channels.
source: Finally, the spontaneous bursting pattern of activity is usually absent from mature SNc DA neurons in vitro, but can be observed in juvenile neurons (P15–P21) and depends on the activation of NMDA receptors (Mereu et al., 1997), or can be promoted by pharmacological blockade of T-type calcium channels and SK potassium channels (Wolfart and Roeper, 2002).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study describing pharmacological induction of bursting.

claim: All experiments were performed according to the European and institutional guidelines for the care and use of laboratory animals (Council Directive 86/609/EEC and French National Research Council).
source: All experiments were performed according to the European and institutional guidelines for the care and use of laboratory animals (Council Directive 86/609/EEC and French National Research Council).
evidence: The manuscript states compliance with ethical guidelines.

claim: Recordings were performed on midbrain slices continuously superfused with oxygenated aCSF at 30–32°C.
source: All recordings (315 cells from 120 rats) were performed on midbrain slices continuously superfused with oxygenated aCSF at 30–32°C.
evidence: The manuscript describes the recording conditions.

claim: Picrotoxin and Kynurenate were systematically present for all recordings to prevent contamination of the intrinsic activity by spontaneous glutamatergic and GABAergic synaptic activity.
source: Picrotoxin and Kynurenate were systematically present for all recordings to prevent contamination of the intrinsic activity by spontaneous glutamatergic and GABAergic synaptic activity.
evidence: The manuscript describes the pharmacological conditions used in all recordings.

claim: A significant proportion of SNc dopaminergic neurons intrinsically generate calcium spikes or calcium plateaus between E16 and P0, while this calcium activity strongly decreases by P7.
source: Interestingly, a very recent study using calcium imaging demonstrated that a significant proportion of SNc dopaminergic neurons intrinsically generate calcium spikes or calcium plateaus between E16 and P0, while this calcium activity strongly decreases by P7 (Ferrari et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites a recent study describing calcium activity in early development.

claim: Bursting behavior usually relies on the activation of calcium conductances, including L-type calcium channels in SNc dopaminergic neurons.
source: Since bursting behavior usually relies on the activation of calcium conductances (Destexhe and Sejnowski, 2003), including L-type calcium channels in SNc dopaminergic neurons (Johnson and Wu, 2004), our observation that most SNc dopaminergic neurons at P2–P3 are intrinsic bursters corroborates the findings of Ferrari et al., (2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies describing the biophysical basis of bursting.

claim: Midbrain dopaminergic neurons already project to the striatum at embryonic stage E16 and release dopamine at E18.
source: While midbrain dopaminergic neurons already project to the striatum at embryonic stage E16 and release dopamine at E18 (Hu et al., 2004; Ferrari et al., 2012), the refinement of their projections continues at least until P0 (Hu et al., 2004), and it is likely that this pruning involves calcium-dependent mechanisms.
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies describing early development of dopaminergic projections.

claim: The refinement of dopaminergic projections continues at least until P0.
source: While midbrain dopaminergic neurons already project to the striatum at embryonic stage E16 and release dopamine at E18 (Hu et al., 2004; Ferrari et al., 2012), the refinement of their projections continues at least until P0 (Hu et al., 2004), and it is likely that this pruning involves calcium-dependent mechanisms.
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study describing projection refinement.

claim: It is likely that projection pruning involves calcium-dependent mechanisms.
source: While midbrain dopaminergic neurons already project to the striatum at embryonic stage E16 and release dopamine at E18 (Hu et al., 2004; Ferrari et al., 2012), the refinement of their projections continues at least until P0 (Hu et al., 2004), and it is likely that this pruning involves calcium-dependent mechanisms.
evidence: The manuscript speculates about the mechanism of projection refinement based on general knowledge.

claim: The intrinsic bursting observed in SNc dopaminergic neurons at early postnatal stages may promote calcium-dependent projection refinement.
source: The intrinsic bursting observed in SNc dopaminergic neurons at early postnatal stages may promote this process.
evidence: The manuscript speculates about the functional role of early bursting activity.

claim: Regular tonic activity relies on many different voltage-dependent intrinsic conductances, including transient sodium currents.
source: From a biophysical point of view, regular tonic activity relies on many different voltage-dependent intrinsic conductances, including transient sodium currents (Puopolo et al., 2007; Guzman et al., 2009; Drion et al., 2011; Tucker et al., 2012), high and low voltage-activated calcium currents (Chan et al., 2007; Puopolo et al., 2007; Guzman et al., 2009; Putzier et al., 2009a), transient potassium currents (Liss et al., 2001; Hahn et al., 2003; Putzier et al., 2009b; Amendola et al., 2012), and hyperpolarization-activated currents (Seutin et al., 2001; Neuhoff et al., 2002; Chan et al., 2007; Tateno and Robinson, 2011), while the irregular pattern of activity observed in juvenile animals seems to be strongly dependent on the sporadic activation of the apamin-sensitive SK currents via the spontaneous activation of T-type calcium channels (Seutin et al., 1998; Cui et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple previous studies describing the ionic basis of regular tonic activity.

claim: Regular tonic activity relies on high and low voltage-activated calcium currents.
source: From a biophysical point of view, regular tonic activity relies on many different voltage-dependent intrinsic conductances, including transient sodium currents (Puopolo et al., 2007; Guzman et al., 2009; Drion et al., 2011; Tucker et al., 2012), high and low voltage-activated calcium currents (Chan et al., 2007; Puopolo et al., 2007; Guzman et al., 2009; Putzier et al., 2009a), transient potassium currents (Liss et al., 2001; Hahn et al., 2003; Putzier et al., 2009b; Amendola et al., 2012), and hyperpolarization-activated currents (Seutin et al., 2001; Neuhoff et al., 2002; Chan et al., 2007; Tateno and Robinson, 2011), while the irregular pattern of activity observed in juvenile animals seems to be strongly dependent on the sporadic activation of the apamin-sensitive SK currents via the spontaneous activation of T-type calcium channels (Seutin et al., 1998; Cui et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies describing the ionic basis of regular tonic activity.

claim: Regular tonic activity relies on transient potassium currents.
source: From a biophysical point of view, regular tonic activity relies on many different voltage-dependent intrinsic conductances, including transient sodium currents (Puopolo et al., 2007; Guzman et al., 2009; Drion et al., 2011; Tucker et al., 2012), high and low voltage-activated calcium currents (Chan et al., 2007; Puopolo et al., 2007; Guzman et al., 2009; Putzier et al., 2009a), transient potassium currents (Liss et al., 2001; Hahn et al., 2003; Putzier et al., 2009b; Amendola et al., 2012), and hyperpolarization-activated currents (Seutin et al., 2001; Neuhoff et al., 2002; Chan et al., 2007; Tateno and Robinson, 2011), while the irregular pattern of activity observed in juvenile animals seems to be strongly dependent on the sporadic activation of the apamin-sensitive SK currents via the spontaneous activation of T-type calcium channels (Seutin et al., 1998; Cui et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies describing the ionic basis of regular tonic activity.

claim: Regular tonic activity relies on hyperpolarization-activated currents.
source: From a biophysical point of view, regular tonic activity relies on many different voltage-dependent intrinsic conductances, including transient sodium currents (Puopolo et al., 2007; Guzman et al., 2009; Drion et al., 2011; Tucker et al., 2012), high and low voltage-activated calcium currents (Chan et al., 2007; Puopolo et al., 2007; Guzman et al., 2009; Putzier et al., 2009a), transient potassium currents (Liss et al., 2001; Hahn et al., 2003; Putzier et al., 2009b; Amendola et al., 2012), and hyperpolarization-activated currents (Seutin et al., 2001; Neuhoff et al., 2002; Chan et al., 2007; Tateno and Robinson, 2011), while the irregular pattern of activity observed in juvenile animals seems to be strongly dependent on the sporadic activation of the apamin-sensitive SK currents via the spontaneous activation of T-type calcium channels (Seutin et al., 1998; Cui et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies describing the ionic basis of regular tonic activity.

claim: SK currents have been demonstrated to control the regularity of spontaneous activity in SNc dopaminergic neurons from both juvenile and mature animals in vitro.
source: In fact, SK currents have been demonstrated to control the regularity of spontaneous activity in SNc dopaminergic neurons from both juvenile and mature animals in vitro (Ping and Shepard, 1996; Wolfart et al., 2001).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies describing the role of SK currents in firing regularity.

claim: SK current activation seems to be essential to the regular tonic pattern of activity as blockade of SK currents, under specific experimental conditions, induces a switch to a bursting pattern of activity, both in vitro and in vivo.
source: Moreover, SK current activation seems to be essential to the regular tonic pattern of activity as blockade of SK currents, under specific experimental conditions, induces a switch to a bursting pattern of activity, both in vitro (Wolfart and Roeper, 2002; Johnson and Wu, 2004) and in vivo (Waroux et al., 2005).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies describing the effect of SK current blockade.

claim: SNc dopaminergic neurons were shown to reach morphological maturity by P14, since neither soma size nor cell area change significantly from P14 to adulthood.
source: The electrophysiological measurements of passive properties (input resistance, membrane capacitance, membrane time constant) we obtained in the current study extend previous results on the morphological changes of SNc dopaminergic neurons during postnatal development: SNc dopaminergic neurons were shown to reach morphological maturity by P14, since neither soma size (Tepper et al., 1994) nor cell area (Park et al., 2000) change significantly from P14 to adulthood.
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies describing morphological development.

claim: The drop in input resistance observed during the first two postnatal weeks counteracts the reported increase in IH amplitude, such that sag amplitude and rebound delay remain constant.
source: Our current interpretation is that the drop in input resistance observed during the same timeframe counteracts the reported increase in IH amplitude (Washio et al., 1999), such that sag amplitude and rebound delay remain constant.
evidence: The manuscript provides an interpretation of the data based on biophysical principles.

claim: Previously published studies on SNc dopaminergic neurons have described a monophasic increase in AP amplitude associated with an increase in AP rise slope over the first two postnatal weeks.
source: So far, previously published studies on SNc dopaminergic neurons have described more classical changes in these parameters over the same time range, that is, a monophasic increase in amplitude associated with an increase in AP rise slope (or the subsequent decrease in AP half-width) (Washio et al., 1999; Ferrari et al., 2012), although fewer developmental stages and smaller samples were analyzed compared to the current study.
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies describing AP development.

claim: Previous studies dedicated to mouse cerebral cortex and hippocampus development described a monophasic increase in AP amplitude and acceleration of the AP.
source: Nevertheless, previous studies dedicated to mouse cerebral cortex and hippocampus development described the same type of monophasic increase in amplitude and acceleration of the AP (McCormick and Prince, 1987; Spigelman et al., 1992; Picken Bahrey and Moody, 2003; Williams and Sutherland, 2004).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies from other brain regions for comparison.

claim: The monophasic increase in AP amplitude and acceleration was due to an increase in the amplitude of the transient sodium current over the first two postnatal weeks.
source: One of these studies demonstrated that it was due to an increase in the amplitude of the transient sodium current over the first two postnatal weeks (Picken Bahrey and Moody, 2003), consistent with the role of this current in defining the rise kinetics and the amplitude of the AP (Bean, 2007).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study describing the mechanism of AP development.

claim: The axon initial segment (AIS), the main site of AP initiation, is located at highly variable distances from the soma (between 0 and 250 µm) in mature SNc dopaminergic neurons.
source: For instance, it is known that the axon initial segment (AIS), the main site of AP initiation, is located at highly variable distances from the soma (between 0 and 250 µm) in mature SNc dopaminergic neurons (Hausser et al., 1995).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study describing AIS location variability.

claim: Mild changes in the location of the AIS can significantly influence the response of the neuron to sensory inputs or current injection.
source: Recent studies have demonstrated that mild changes in the location of the AIS can significantly influence the response of the neuron to sensory inputs (Kuba et al., 2006, 2010) or current injection (Grubb and Burrone, 2010a, 2010b).
evidence: The manuscript cites recent studies describing the functional significance of AIS location.

claim: Multivariate analyses such as PCA are designed to solve the problem of analyzing many distinct properties that do not co-vary by compressing the number of meaningful parameters.
source: While multivariate analyses such as PCA are designed to solve that problem by compressing the number of meaningful parameters (see next section), we propose an intermediate solution which consists of a visual stacking of the results of the uni-variate analyses performed on each parameter.
evidence: The manuscript describes the purpose and function of PCA based on established statistical knowledge.

claim: Dimensional stacking entails visualizing a high-dimensional data set in a two-dimensional space and has been recently applied to analyze the electrical behavior of databases of complex realistic neuron models.
source: Dimensional stacking entails visualizing a high-dimensional data set in a two-dimensional space and has been recently applied to analyze the electrical behavior of databases of complex realistic neuron models (Taylor et al., 2006).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study that used dimensional stacking.

claim: Multivariate analyses, and in particular clustering analysis, have been mainly used in neurophysiology to classify and distinguish mature neuronal populations.
source: So far, multivariate analyses, and in particular clustering analysis, have been mainly used in neurophysiology to classify and distinguish mature neuronal populations (Ascoli et al., 2008; Karagiannis et al., 2009; McGarry et al., 2010; Laramee et al., 2013; Simonnet et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies that used multivariate analyses for neuronal classification.

claim: Research dedicated to the classification of cortical interneuron subpopulations has led to the creation of an international consortium (the Petilla Interneuron Nomenclature Group).
source: For instance, research dedicated to the classification of cortical interneuron subpopulations (for review see Ascoli et al., 2008; Defelipe et al., 2013) has led to the creation of an international consortium (the Petilla Interneuron Nomenclature Group).
evidence: The manuscript cites reviews describing the classification efforts for cortical interneurons.

claim: Classification of cortical interneurons often relies on the use of hierarchical clustering analysis or similar techniques applied to a combination of morphological, molecular, and electrophysiological criteria.
source: This type of classification often relies on the use of hierarchical clustering analysis or similar techniques applied to a combination of morphological (axon and dendrite length and shape…), molecular (expression of specific genes), and electrophysiological (frequency of spiking, frequency adaptation…) criteria (Karagiannis et al., 2009; Battaglia et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies describing classification methods for cortical interneurons.

claim: Principal component analysis has been used to analyze the diversity of cortical interneurons or the anatomical differences of cortical principal neurons between different cortical areas.
source: Principal component analysis has also been used to analyze the diversity of cortical interneurons (McGarry et al., 2010) or the anatomical differences of cortical principal neurons between different cortical areas (Laramee et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies that used PCA for neuronal analysis.

claim: AHC and PCA can be efficiently applied to the analysis of developmental changes in electrical behavior in a given population of neurons.
source: In the current study, we show that AHC and PCA can also be efficiently applied to the analysis of developmental changes in electrical behavior in a given population of neurons.
evidence: The manuscript demonstrates a novel application of multivariate analyses.

claim: The variability in phenotype was decreasing across development.
source: The multi-variate analyses we performed not only revealed that the electrical phenotype of SNc dopaminergic neurons was following a biphasic trajectory, it also revealed that the variability in phenotype was decreasing across development (Figure 10).
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing decreasing phenotypic variability.

claim: The observation of decreasing phenotypic variability is consistent with the idea of canalization of development formulated by Conrad Hal Waddington.
source: This observation is particularly interesting and consistent with the idea of canalization of development formulated by the English embryologist Conrad Hal Waddington (Waddington, 1942, 1957; Debat and David, 2001).
evidence: The manuscript cites Waddington's theory to interpret the findings.

claim: Waddington postulated that in a canalised system, trajectories starting from any point within a certain volume will converge to a single end point which is the corresponding steady-state.
source: In this theory, Waddington postulated the following, referring in particular to organ development: 'In a canalised system of the kind we have been considering, trajectories starting from any point within a certain volume will converge to a single end point which is the corresponding steady-state…' (Waddington, 1957).
evidence: The manuscript quotes Waddington's theory.

claim: The variability in phenotype (and the corresponding region of the PCA space) is much larger at early developmental stages (P2–P5) than at late developmental stages where all values cluster in a single point of space.
source: This precisely describes what is occurring with SNc dopaminergic neuron's phenotype as defined in the PCA space: the variability in phenotype (and the corresponding region of the PCA space) is much larger at early developmental stages (P2–P5) than at late developmental stages where all values cluster in a single point of space (Figures 9C and 10).
evidence: The manuscript describes how the data fit Waddington's theory.

claim: Neurons may be very heterogeneous early in development and then use flexible developmental trajectories to reach a highly 'attractive' mature phenotype.
source: This suggests that neurons may be very heterogeneous early in development and then use flexible developmental trajectories to reach a highly 'attractive' mature phenotype.
evidence: The manuscript infers a developmental principle from the data.

claim: Mature neurons generate highly similar patterns of activity using variable solutions of underlying conductances, commonly displaying twofold to fourfold ranges of expression/amplitude of ion channels/currents.
source: Previous studies have shown that mature neurons generate highly similar patterns of activity using variable solutions of underlying conductances, commonly displaying twofold to fourfold ranges of expression/amplitude of ion channels/currents (Marder and Goaillard, 2006; Schulz et al., 2006, 2007; Goaillard et al., 2009; Taylor et al., 2009; Amendola et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies describing variability in ion channel expression.

claim: Mature SNc dopaminergic neurons can generate regular tonic activity patterns of similar frequencies while displaying substantial differences in the amplitude and gating properties of IA and IH.
source: For instance, mature SNc dopaminergic neurons can generate regular tonic activity patterns of similar frequencies while displaying substantial differences in the amplitude and gating properties of IA and IH (Amendola et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study describing variability in SNc dopaminergic neurons.

claim: Immature neurons, showing heterogeneous phenotypes, may display even larger variability in their underlying conductances.
source: These findings may imply that immature neurons, showing heterogeneous phenotypes, display even larger variability in their underlying conductances.
evidence: The manuscript infers greater variability in immature neurons from the phenotypic data.

claim: The developmental profiles of ion channel expression rapidly change over the first two postnatal weeks, as has been shown in many systems, including the SNc dopaminergic neurons.
source: The developmental profiles of ion channel expression rapidly change over the first two postnatal weeks, as has been shown in many systems (Moody and Bosma, 2005), including the SNc dopaminergic neurons (Washio et al., 1999; Dufour et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies describing developmental changes in ion channel expression.

claim: Slight differences in the developmental timecourses of neurons would certainly exacerbate the cell-to-cell variability in expression of ion channels already observed in mature neurons, and would reveal even larger ranges of expression of ion channels in immature neurons.
source: Slight differences in the developmental timecourses of neurons (visible only at early developmental stages) would certainly exacerbate the cell-to-cell variability in expression of ion channels already observed in mature neurons, and would reveal even larger ranges of expression of ion channels in immature neurons.
evidence: The manuscript speculates about the mechanism underlying greater variability in immature neurons.

claim: The first transition (P3 to P5) involves a dramatic concomitant increase in leak conductance.
source: While the increase in calcium-activated potassium current is involved in both transitions, the first transition (P3 to P5) involves a dramatic concomittant increase in leak conductance whereas the second transition (P9 to P11) may rely on a concomittant increase in fast sodium conductance.
evidence: The manuscript describes the biophysical mechanisms underlying the first developmental transition based on experimental data.

claim: The second transition (P9 to P11) may rely on a concomitant increase in fast sodium conductance.
source: While the increase in calcium-activated potassium current is involved in both transitions, the first transition (P3 to P5) involves a dramatic concomittant increase in leak conductance whereas the second transition (P9 to P11) may rely on a concomittant increase in fast sodium conductance.
evidence: The manuscript describes the biophysical mechanisms underlying the second developmental transition based on experimental data.

claim: Manipulating leak, sodium, and calcium-activated potassium currents quantitatively reproduces the changes in electrical phenotype observed between developmental stages.
source: Although we cannot conclude that these biophysical mechanisms are the only ones involved in these developmental transitions, our experiments demonstrate that manipulating these parameters quantitatively reproduces the changes in electrical phenotype observed between these stages (see Figure 11E).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing that specific manipulations reproduce developmental changes.
